enonce_markdown: A nurse at a health centre in Bamenda measures a patient's body temperature and obtains $37\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Express this temperature on the Kelvin scale.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The Kelvin and Celsius scales have degrees of the same size, but the Kelvin scale starts at absolute zero. So $T/\mathrm{K} = \theta/^\circ\mathrm{C} + 273$.

### Solution

$T = 37 + 273 = 310\ \mathrm{K}$.

The other values come from typical mistakes: $37\ \mathrm{K}$ (no conversion at all), $236\ \mathrm{K}$ (the 273 was subtracted instead of added) and $373\ \mathrm{K}$ (which is the boiling point of water, $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$, not the body temperature). **Answer: c.**

enonce_markdown: Two metal blocks are placed in contact and insulated from their surroundings. Block A is at $80\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ and block B is at $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. Which statement describes what happens?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Heat is energy that flows spontaneously from a region of higher temperature to a region of lower temperature, and the flow stops when both bodies are at the same temperature (thermal equilibrium).

### Solution

Block A is hotter than block B, so heat flows from A to B. The flow continues until the two blocks reach the same temperature, at which point there is no net transfer. Heat does not flow from the colder to the hotter block, a body does not "lose all its heat" (it keeps internal energy at any temperature above absolute zero), and solids conduct heat well. **Answer: d.**

choix.texte: Heat flows from B to A until both blocks reach the same temperature.
Heat flows from A to B until block A has lost all of its heat.
No heat flows because both blocks are solids.
Heat flows from A to B until both blocks reach the same temperature.

enonce_markdown: An aluminium block of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ is heated from $25\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $65\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The specific heat capacity of aluminium is $900\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$. How much heat energy does the block absorb?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

The heat needed to change the temperature of a body is $Q = mc\Delta\theta$, where $\Delta\theta$ is the **change** in temperature (final minus initial).

### Solution

$\Delta\theta = 65 - 25 = 40\ \mathrm{K}$.

$Q = mc\Delta\theta = 0.50\ \mathrm{kg} \times 900\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}} \times 40\ \mathrm{K} = 18\,000\ \mathrm{J}$.

Wrong options: $450\ \mathrm{J}$ forgets $\Delta\theta$; $29\,250\ \mathrm{J}$ uses the final temperature $65$ instead of the change; $40\,500\ \mathrm{J}$ adds the two temperatures. **Answer: b.**

enonce_markdown:
An immersion heater rated $1.5\ \mathrm{kW}$ is used to heat $2.0\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water in a bucket from $24\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ to $84\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The specific heat capacity of water is $4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

(a) Calculate the heat energy gained by the water.

(b) Assuming that all the energy from the heater goes into the water, calculate the time taken.

(c) State why the real heating time is longer than your answer to (b).
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Heat gained by a substance: $Q = mc\Delta\theta$. Energy supplied by a heater: $E = Pt$ (power in watts, time in seconds). With no losses, $Pt = mc\Delta\theta$.

### Solution

(a) $\Delta\theta = 84 - 24 = 60\ \mathrm{K}$, so $Q = mc\Delta\theta = 2.0 \times 4200 \times 60 = 504\,000\ \mathrm{J}$ ($5.04 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$).

(b) The power must be in watts: $P = 1.5\ \mathrm{kW} = 1500\ \mathrm{W}$. From $Pt = Q$:

$t = \dfrac{Q}{P} = \dfrac{504\,000\ \mathrm{J}}{1500\ \mathrm{W}} = 336\ \mathrm{s}$, that is $5.6$ minutes.

(c) Some of the energy is lost to the bucket and to the surrounding air, so the heater must run longer to deliver the same $504\,000\ \mathrm{J}$ to the water.

enonce_markdown: A fish seller in Douala puts $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ of ice at $0\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$ in a cooler box. The specific latent heat of fusion of ice is $3.4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}}$. How much heat is needed to melt all the ice without changing its temperature?
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

Changing state at constant temperature needs $Q = ml$, where $l$ is the specific latent heat. No $\Delta\theta$ is involved because the temperature stays the same while the ice melts.

### Solution

$Q = ml = 0.40\ \mathrm{kg} \times 3.4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}} = 1.36 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$.

Wrong options: $3.4 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$ forgets the mass; $8.5 \times 10^{5}\ \mathrm{J}$ divides $l$ by $m$; $1.36 \times 10^{8}\ \mathrm{J}$ uses $400$ (grams) with a constant given per kilogram. **Answer: a.**

enonce_markdown:
A metal block of mass $0.50\ \mathrm{kg}$ is heated in boiling water until it is at $100\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. It is quickly transferred into an insulated container holding $0.40\ \mathrm{kg}$ of water at $20\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The final steady temperature of the water and block is $30\,^\circ\mathrm{C}$. The specific heat capacity of water is $4200\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$ and the heat capacity of the container can be ignored.

(a) Calculate the heat gained by the water.

(b) Calculate the specific heat capacity of the metal.

(c) State one reason why the value you calculated is likely to be lower than the true value of the metal.
corrige_markdown:
### Method reminder

In a mixture with no heat loss, heat lost by the hot body = heat gained by the cold body, where each is $mc\Delta\theta$ with $\Delta\theta$ taken as a positive temperature difference.

### Solution

(a) Water: $\Delta\theta = 30 - 20 = 10\ \mathrm{K}$, so
$Q_{\text{gained}} = 0.40 \times 4200 \times 10 = 16\,800\ \mathrm{J}$.

(b) Metal: $\Delta\theta = 100 - 30 = 70\ \mathrm{K}$. Heat lost by the metal $= 0.50 \times c \times 70 = 35c$. Heat lost = heat gained:

$35c = 16\,800 \Rightarrow c = \dfrac{16\,800}{35} = 480\ \mathrm{J\,kg^{-1}\,K^{-1}}$.

(c) Some heat is lost while the block is transferred and some is lost to the container and the air, so the water gains less than the metal gives out. The measured final temperature is then too low, and the calculation under-estimates the quantity of heat the metal gave out. (Other accepted answers: the block carried some boiling water with it, or heat was lost during stirring.)
